beliefs.practice: Read the MongoDB-compatible connection string from an environment variable (DOCUMENTDB_URI) at runtime; never hard-code or commit credentials. Use a secrets store (Azure Key Vault) in production to supply that URI.

Open a single shared Mongoose/MongoDB client (connection pool) per Node process and reuse it; configure pool options such as maxPoolSize (e.g. 50) and socketTimeoutMS/connectTimeoutMS rather than creating new connections per request.
Enable TLS in the connection string (mongodb+srv or tls=true) and ensure server certificate validation is not disabled in production.

Create compound indexes with equality fields first, then sort/range fields. For history queries create indexes exactly: { customerId: 1, timestamp: -1 } and { channel: 1, timestamp: -1 } (timestamp descending supports recent-first).

Do not rely on skip-based pagination for large offsets; implement cursor-based pagination using the compound index (e.g. query customerId = X AND (timestamp < lastTimestamp OR (timestamp = lastTimestamp AND _id < lastId)) sorted by timestamp desc, _id desc) and return an opaque nextCursor token.

Make seeding idempotent by using updateOne(..., { upsert: true }) or bulkWrite with upsert operations and a unique key (e.g. externalInteractionId or a deterministic _id) to avoid duplicates on repeated runs.
Validate and store timestamps in UTC ISODate (JavaScript Date) and index the timestamp field; never store local-time strings for time-range queries.

Use a JSON Schema / collection validator or Mongoose schema to enforce required fields (customerId, channel, timestamp, content/embedding) at write time to prevent schema drift in a single collection storing multiple channel types.
Disable Mongoose/MongoDB autoIndex in production (autoIndex: false) and create indexes explicitly during deployment or as an idempotent migration script to avoid runtime indexing overhead.

When using vector fields/embeddings, store vectors as an array of numbers of the expected dimensionality and create the cluster vector index with matching dimension and index type (HNSW/IVF) — validate vector length on write to match index configuration.

Use partial indexes or sparse indexes if only a subset of documents contain a field (e.g. embedding) to avoid indexing large unused fields: e.g. createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { partialFilterExpression: { embedding: { $exists: true } } }) where supported.
Protect against rate-limiting (429) and transient network errors by implementing retries with exponential backoff and jitter; read Retry-After/Retry-After-ms when available and back off accordingly.

Keep documents small — avoid embedding large blobs (images/audio). If attachments are needed, store them in blob/object storage and keep only references in the document; aim to stay well under typical document size limits (MongoDB 16MB guidance).
Use projection (select only needed fields) on queries and aggregations to reduce RU consumption and network payload — e.g. projection { content: 1, timestamp: 1, channel: 1 } for history lists.

Monitor RU/s consumption and tune queries and indexes accordingly; use explain() or the MCP tooling to verify query plans use the intended compound indexes and to measure RU charge for representative queries.

For aggregation endpoints (channel breakdown), use the aggregation pipeline with $match (indexed fields), then $group and $sort; restrict the match by indexed fields (channel or customerId and time range) so the pipeline is RU-efficient.

Implement request-level timeouts and sensible serverSelectionTimeoutMS/connectTimeoutMS so app requests fail fast if the cluster is unreachable rather than accumulating queued requests occupying the pool.
Use acknowledged writes and idempotent operations for retry safety — for example, use upsert or deduplication keys and avoid unbounded retries of non-idempotent inserts.

If you need automatic data expiration, use a TTL index on the timestamp field or container-level TTL where supported to expire old interactions, and verify how TTL is implemented in the MongoDB API of the service.

Protect against schema drift in a single collection used by many channels by including a lightweight 'channel' discriminator and consider partial projections or polymorphic subdocuments; plan indexes around queries (channel + timestamp) rather than per-channel collections unless very different access patterns require separation.
Use explain() for sample queries during development to confirm the created compound indexes are being used and to detect COLLSCANs; examine index keys, numberExamined, and RU or time cost.
Avoid creating overly broad wildcard indexes; only index fields that support the query patterns (customerId, channel, timestamp, embedding (vector) when used), to conserve RU and storage.

When running aggregation or heavy read workloads, consider scaling RU/s (or enabling autoscale) for the container to prevent throttling, and set a reasonable maxTimeMS for queries to avoid runaway queries that waste RU.

Make index creation idempotent in setup scripts (createIndexes or ensureIndex) and avoid dropping and recreating indexes in production unless necessary; run index creation during a maintenance window if it impacts RU.
Return minimal error details to callers (avoid leaking connection strings or internal diagnostics); log rich diagnostics (stack, query plan, RU charge) to trusted logs/monitoring only.
